summary: This RFC updates the IANA registries of RFC 4255, which defines the SSHFP DNS record holding SSH host key fingerprints. It adds ECDSA keys and SHA-256 fingerprints.

eli5.summary: A DNS record holds a fingerprint of a server's key. This adds a newer key type and a stronger fingerprint method.

questions: ssh host key fingerprint in dns
subtitle: Two new numbers for SSHFP DNS records: one for ECDSA keys and one for SHA-256 fingerprints.

tldr.problem: SSHFP records publish SSH host key fingerprints in DNS, but they had no way to say that a key is ECDSA or that the fingerprint was made with SHA-256.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds algorithm number 3 for ECDSA public keys and fingerprint type 2 for SHA-256 fingerprints, and says how implementations should prefer and handle them.
tldr.outcome: SSH clients that look up host keys in DNSSEC-signed DNS can use ECDSA keys and the stronger SHA-256 digest instead of only SHA-1.

today: RFC 6594 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the SSHFP values for ECDSA and SHA-256 and builds on RFC 4255.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SSHFP resource record, defined in RFC 4255, stores a fingerprint of an SSH server's public key in DNS. A client can then check the key the server presents against the fingerprint it finds in the DNS, using DNSSEC to verify the lookup.

Each SSHFP record holds the fingerprint plus two index numbers. One identifies the public key algorithm, which links the fingerprinted key to its private key. The other identifies the message digest algorithm that produced the fingerprint. RFC 4255 lists the algorithms and their numbers.

This RFC adds one entry to each list: the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) for keys, and SHA-256 for fingerprints. The text assumes you already know DNSSEC, SSH, SSHFP and the SHA-2 family.
sections.eli5: A computer can publish a short code for its secret key in a public phone book. Both the way of naming the key and the way of making the short code each have a numbered list, and this adds one new item to each.

sections.title: The Two New Values
sections.content:
The record format itself is unchanged and still comes from RFC 4255. This RFC only defines two new numbers.

  • Fingerprint type 2 means the fingerprint of the public key was computed with SHA-256.
  • Algorithm number 3 means the public key is an ECDSA key.

The fingerprint type octet says which message digest algorithm was used. The algorithm number octet says which kind of public key the record describes.
sections.eli5: Each record has two little number tags. Tag 2 on the code says it was made the stronger way, and tag 3 on the key says it is the newer kind of key.

sections.title: What Implementations Should Do
sections.content:
SSHFP-aware SSH implementations SHOULD support SHA-256 fingerprints for verifying the public key. If an implementation does support them, it MUST prefer a SHA-256 fingerprint over SHA-1 when both are available for a server.

There is a strict rule for a mismatch: if the SHA-256 fingerprint is tested and does not match the key received from the SSH server, the key MUST be rejected. The client must not fall back to testing the SHA-1 fingerprint, since that would let an attacker pick the weaker check.

Implementations that support ECDSA for the SSH public key SHOULD also support SSHFP fingerprints for ECDSA keys.
sections.eli5: If a server shows two codes, a strong one and a weak one, check the strong one. If the strong one does not match, do not give it a second chance with the weak one. Just say no.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives an RSA key, a DSA key and an ECDSA key, each in OpenSSH public key format, and shows the SSHFP record for each with a SHA-1 fingerprint and with a SHA-256 fingerprint. The records are written for the host server.example.net.

The two numbers after SSHFP are the algorithm and the fingerprint type. RSA uses 1, DSA uses 2 and ECDSA uses 3, so the ECDSA key with a SHA-256 fingerprint is SSHFP 3 2. SHA-1 fingerprints use type 1.
sections.eli5: The examples show the same three keys written down with the old short code and the new stronger one, so you can see the number tags in action.

sections.title: IANA Registry Updates
sections.content: Two IANA registries were updated. In the registry "SSHFP RR Types for public key algorithms", value 3 was added with the description ECDSA. In the registry "SSHFP RR types for fingerprint types", value 2 was added with the description SHA-256. Both entries reference this document.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of what each number means. This RFC asked for the new numbers to be written into it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations in RFC 4255 for SSHFP records and in RFC 5656 for ECDSA, and adds advice about the digest. Users of SSHFP are encouraged to deploy SHA-256 as soon as implementations allow it.

The SHA-2 family is widely believed to be more resilient to attack than SHA-1, and confidence in SHA-1 was being eroded by recently announced attacks. The RFC says that regardless of whether those attacks affect SSHFP, SHA-256 is believed to be the better choice. It also says SHA-256 is considered sufficiently strong for the immediate future, and that predicting later developments in cryptography is beyond its scope.
sections.eli5: The old way of making the short code is starting to look a little wobbly, so people are asked to move to the sturdier one as soon as their software can.
